The ten cities get the same analysis as Wake County’s two points, on the road network around them, and Dijkstra’s procedure then gives a ten by ten matrix: only the distances between pairs of the ten cities are wanted, not those between the individual road nodes. From Cary, node 1, to Charlotte, node 2, the road distance, connectors included, is below 1.2 times the great circle distance, and in 2024 Google Maps gave 162 miles, higher still and about 30 miles more than the road distance found then. That is a significant difference, and worth asking why. Minimizing distance, the procedure takes the route in red in Fig. 16, which is the shortest route by distance. The routes Google Maps recommended, on I-40 or on US 64 and US 421, were both a lot longer, because Google Maps is looking at travel time: it finds the route with the shortest travel time and does not even consider the shortest distance, whereas the only weight given here was distance.

The procedure did what it is supposed to do: it minimized distance, using whichever roads in the network give the shortest route. To duplicate Google Maps, the distance would be translated into time, which would more likely give the I-40 route, and that is the subject of Sec. 5.

## 5. Travel time

From Cary to Charlotte, Google Maps recommended a much longer route than the shortest one of Ex. 2 because it was minimizing time: it could travel a lot faster on I-40 and I-85 than on US 64 through all of the smaller towns. Minimizing time instead of distance changes only the weight on each arc, and Logjam’s functions are built to allow it. prune_reindex and addconnectors require no fixed column names: they work with the first three columns of the node and link data frames by position, so that different data sources can be used without renaming every column. For the nodes, the first column is the index, followed by the longitude and the latitude; for the links, the first is the source node, the second the destination, and the third the weight, labeled here as distance. To minimize time, the third column would hold a time instead, labeled however is convenient, and pruning and the rest would still work; generically it could be called the weight.

The next step converts the road distances to travel times, since most often the path wanted is not the shortest in distance but the shortest in travel time. The conversion rests on an estimate of the average speed of travel along each link. In the 2018 version of this analysis the speeds were estimates of likely reasonable values, which could be adjusted, and which a function would take as parameters, set by how optimistic or pessimistic one is about actual travel times. Rural Interstates were taken at 75 mph, five above a posted limit of 70. Urban roads that are not Interstates were taken at 25 mph: their posted speed is probably 35 to 45 mph, and the 25 accounts for stopping at red lights. An alternative is to include an expected delay explicitly at every node passed through, for its red light, with a speed between nodes of perhaps 45 mph; taking an average speed that includes a reasonable amount of stopping time is the simpler choice. Each link’s time is its distance divided by its speed, and that time replaces the distance as the link’s weight. A connector, from a facility such as a distribution center, a manufacturing facility or a customer location, was given an average speed of about 20 mph. Connectors joining two facilities directly were ignored: as long as the road network is reasonably dense, travel from one facility to another can be assumed to use it. Only on a sparse network such as the Interstates alone, with areas of the country that have no Interstate, would they be relevant.

The other two speeds were 65 mph on urban Interstates and 50 mph on rural roads that are not Interstates.

An estimate of travel time over a long trip can be remarkably accurate, to within a few minutes even with heavy traffic and construction along the way, unless there is a large delay such as an accident. The reason is the law of large numbers. A long trip is made up of many small road segments, each an opportunity for its estimate to be a little over or a little under, and when the estimates of all of the segments are added up, the overestimates and underestimates tend to balance out. That holds only if the errors on the segments are independent. Segments far apart from each other can reliably be assumed to be, unless an accident were so large that its delay extended over the entire trip.

Connectors pose one problem for speed. Their distance is estimated, as the great circle distance times 1.3, the circuity taken for connectors, but there is no speed for them at all. From a home to a major road of the highway system, the trip is not going to average 60 mph down a residential street: the actual travel speed is perhaps 35 mph at best, and averaging in the time spent waiting at stoplights gives something like 25 to 30 mph. The same holds on highways that are not Interstates, such as US 64 heading west out of Raleigh, with all of its red lights. The network model could be extended to model the nodes themselves, with a cost at each node such as the average length of its signal; that is possible for an application that needs it, though it is not needed here.

FAF5 needs no table of speeds, because each of its links carries a free-flow travel time in each direction, AB_TIME from SRC to DST and BA_TIME back, in minutes. A few links carry no time, and for those the time comes from the link’s posted speed, SPEED; a connector, which has neither, is taken at 20 mph, as in 2018. Every link then has a time each way, and the travel times between the ten cities of Ex. 2 follow on the same network:

```julia
# Code block 51: travel times between the cities of Ex. 2, in minutes
con = isequal.(Lc.SOURCE, "CONNECTOR")
# A link's minutes: FAF5's free-flow time t, or, where a link has none,
# 60 d / v at its posted speed v; a connector at 20 mph
mins(t, v, d) = t > 0 ? t : 60d / v
tAB = [c ? 60d / 20 : mins(t, v, d)
       for (c, t, v, d) in zip(con, Lc.AB_TIME, Lc.SPEED, Lc.DIST)]
tBA = [c ? 60d / 20 : mins(t, v, d)
       for (c, t, v, d) in zip(con, Lc.BA_TIME, Lc.SPEED, Lc.DIST)]
fw, bw = Lc.DIR .!= -1, Lc.DIR .!= 1           # as in Code block 45
gT = SimpleWeightedDiGraph([Lc.SRC[fw]; Lc.DST[bw]],
                           [Lc.DST[fw]; Lc.SRC[bw]],
                           [tAB[fw]; tBA[bw]]; combine = min)
T, PT = shortestpaths(gT, n)                   # minutes
round.(T)

```

- 1 Only the times from city to city are wanted, so Dijkstra’s procedure is run from each of the $n$ cities, the first $n$ nodes, and only the first $n$ entries of each result are kept, the $n$ by $n$ matrix T.

Dijkstra’s procedure then runs on the travel times from each city: in 2018, with 16 cities, a 16 by 16 matrix of the shortest travel times, computed in 0.3 s. The whole road network is used to get those times and then thrown away, keeping just the small matrix of times, as Code block 51 keeps the 10 by 10 matrix T. Dijkstra’s procedure also returns the predecessors, which are much larger, since they cover every node of the network, and from them the paths can be extracted. The shortest travel time route is not necessarily the route that is shortest in distance. So the distance of each fastest route cannot be found by running Dijkstra’s procedure on distance; instead, it is added up along the route, as Code block 52 does for every pair of cities.

```julia
# Code block 52: each route measured the other way, along its path
Wd, Wt = weights(g), weights(gT)     # miles and minutes, arc by arc
# segcost gives the weight of each link along a path
DT = [i == j ? 0.0 : sum(segcost(tracepath(PT[i], i, j), Wd))
      for i in 1:n, j in 1:n]        # miles on each fastest route
TD = [i == j ? 0.0 : sum(segcost(tracepath(P[i], i, j), Wt))
      for i in 1:n, j in 1:n]        # minutes on each shortest route
ir = findfirst(==("Raleigh"), df.NAME)
prt(DataFrame("From" => df.NAME[[1, ir]], "To" => df.NAME[2],
              "Shortest, mi" => round.(D[[1, ir], 2], digits = 1),
              "its min" => round.(TD[[1, ir], 2]),
              "Fastest, min" => round.(T[[1, ir], 2]),
              "its mi" => round.(DT[[1, ir], 2], digits = 1)))

```

- 1 The path of the shortest travel time route from city i to city j is taken from the predecessors PT by tracepath, and the distances of its links are added along it, for every pair of cities, to give the distance of each shortest travel time route.

```text
     From         To  Shortest, mi  its min  Fastest, min  its mi
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Cary  Charlotte        131.70      176           172  134.90
  Raleigh  Charlotte        143.50      184           178  169.70
```

For 85 of the 90 ordered pairs of cities, the fastest route is longer than the shortest. From Raleigh to Charlotte, the fastest route is 26.2 mi longer than the shortest and 7 min faster. From Cary to Charlotte, on FAF5’s free-flow times, the fastest route is only 3.1 mi longer than the shortest.

Example 3: High Point to Goldsboro

Determine the shortest route and the fastest route by road from High Point to Goldsboro, and the distance and travel time of each, taking FAF5’s free-flow times on its links and 20 mph on the connectors.

```julia
# Code block 53: High Point to Goldsboro, shortest and fastest
hp = loc2lonlat("High Point"; state = :NC)
gb = loc2lonlat("Goldsboro"; state = :NC)
X, Y = [hp.LON, gb.LON], [hp.LAT, gb.LAT]
N3, L3 = cropnetwork(N, L, X, Y; xexpand = 0.2, yexpand = 0.5)
N3, L3 = addconnectors(N3, L3, X, Y; add_nf_nf = false)
c3 = isequal.(L3.SOURCE, "CONNECTOR")
t3AB = [c ? 60d / 20 : mins(t, v, d)       # minutes, as in Code block 51
        for (c, t, v, d) in zip(c3, L3.AB_TIME, L3.SPEED, L3.DIST)]
t3BA = [c ? 60d / 20 : mins(t, v, d)
        for (c, t, v, d) in zip(c3, L3.BA_TIME, L3.SPEED, L3.DIST)]
fw, bw = L3.DIR .!= -1, L3.DIR .!= 1
I3, J3 = [L3.SRC[fw]; L3.DST[bw]], [L3.DST[fw]; L3.SRC[bw]]
g3 = SimpleWeightedDiGraph(I3, J3, [L3.DIST[fw]; L3.DIST[bw]];
                           combine = min)                  # miles
g3T = SimpleWeightedDiGraph(I3, J3, [t3AB[fw]; t3BA[bw]];
                            combine = min)                 # minutes
pD = tracepath(dijkstra_shortest_paths(g3, 1).parents, 1, 2)   # shortest
pF = tracepath(dijkstra_shortest_paths(g3T, 1).parents, 1, 2)  # fastest
miD = sum.(segcost.([pD, pF], Ref(weights(g3))))   # miles of each
minT = sum.(segcost.([pD, pF], Ref(weights(g3T))))  # minutes of each
# hm, defined with the page's setup, writes minutes as hours and minutes
prt(DataFrame("Route" => ["Shortest", "Fastest"],
              "mi" => round.(miD, digits = 1), "Time" => hm.(minT)))
```

──────────────────────────────

The new nodes are numbered first, so the cities come first in the arc list and every road node has a higher number, which is what lets the path between two cities be read directly. The 2018 version of this example, on the Oak Ridge roads, drew the fastest route from High Point to Goldsboro on the map with the distance and the estimated time in its title. Instead of going through downtown Raleigh, which the short-distance path would do, the fastest route goes around the Beltline, then continues along I-40 to US 70 and over to Goldsboro. It was estimated at 143.5 miles and 2 hours 28 minutes. Google Maps then gave 2 hours 33 minutes for its shortest travel time route, within five minutes of the estimate, at 144 miles, almost exactly the same distance. The estimated times were probably close to what Google Maps uses, even though the speeds were never designed to match it: an assumed average speed must be fairly close to Google’s own. A match is not always this close, but this is the underlying mechanics of what Google Maps does when it solves a problem like this one.

Lecture 2.7, Sec. 3, anticipated an application of set covering, Model 4 in Lecture 2.7, to a road network: the fewest intersections such that every intersection is within a stated reach of a selected one, the selected intersections being truck terminals. Locating transshipment terminals adds one condition, that each terminal lie within a day’s drive of another so that a driver can carry freight between them, and with that condition in the formulation from the start the problem is Model 2, a special case of set covering.

minimize: number of terminals

solve for:
(a) intersections to select as terminals.

subject to:
(a) coverage: every intersection is within half a day’s drive of a terminal;
(b) linehaul: every terminal is within a day’s drive of another terminal.

assumptions:
(a) travel time between two intersections is the time of the shortest path between them;
(b) any intersection can be a terminal.

Model 2: Transshipment terminals

Special case of Model 4: Set covering in Lecture 2.7

Model 2 formulation: Transshipment terminals

$$
\begin{array}{rlrclll}
& \text{Minimize} & \displaystyle \sum_{i \in N} x_i & & & & \\[2pt]
& \text{subject to} & \displaystyle \sum_{\substack{i \in N \,: \\ t_{ij} \le t_{\max}/2}} x_i & \geq & 1, & j \in N & (a) \\[2pt]
& & x_i & \leq & \displaystyle \sum_{\substack{k \in N \setminus \{i\} \,: \\ t_{ik} \le t_{\max}}} x_k, & i \in N & (b) \\[2pt]
& & x_i & \in & \{0,1\}, & i \in N &
\end{array}
\tag{5}
$$

where

- $x_i$ = $\begin{cases} 1, & \text{if intersection } i \text{ is a terminal} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$
- $t_{ij}$ = travel time from intersection $i$ to intersection $j$ (h)
- $t_{\max}$ = longest time a driver may drive in a day (h)
- $N$ = intersections
= $\{1, \ldots, n\}$.

Model 2 states two constraints, and both are rows. Row (a), coverage, is the row of Eq. 9 in Lecture 2.7 with every cost one, intersection $j$ being covered by a terminal at $i$ when $t_{ij} \le t_{\max}/2$, half a day’s drive. Row (b), linehaul, is the row Model 2 adds: an intersection can be selected as a terminal only if another terminal is selected within $t_{\max}$ of it. Its sum is over the set $\{k \in N \setminus \{i\} : t_{ik} \le t_{\max}\}$, read “the $k$ in $N$ other than $i$ such that $t_{ik} \le t_{\max}$”: the colon reads “such that,” as it does under the sum of row (a), and $N \setminus \{i\}$ is the set difference of $N$ and $\{i\}$, the members of $N$ that are not in $\{i\}$, so the sum counts the terminals within $t_{\max}$ of $i$ other than $i$ itself, and the implementation writes the set difference as setdiff(N, [i]). Leaving $i$ out matters: since $t_{ii} = 0$, the sum would otherwise include $x_i$, and the row would hold whatever was selected.

Model 2 implementation: Transshipment terminals

```julia
# Model: transshipment terminals, set covering with a linehaul condition
using JuMP, HiGHS
function terminals(T, tmax)
    N = 1:size(T, 1)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, x[i ∈ N], Bin)
    @objective(model, Min, sum(x[i] for i ∈ N))
    @constraint(model, coverage[j ∈ N],      # (a)
                sum(x[i] for i ∈ N if T[i, j] ≤ tmax / 2) ≥ 1)
    @constraint(model, linehaul[i ∈ N],      # (b)
                x[i] ≤ sum(x[k] for k ∈ setdiff(N, [i])
                                if T[i, k] ≤ tmax))
    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    return findall(==(1.0), snapvals(value.(x)))
end
```

```text
terminals (generic function with 1 method)
```

Example 4: Transshipment terminals

A national less-than-truckload (LTL) carrier would like to know what would be the minimum number of transshipment terminals needed to cover the continental U.S. and their locations. All of their existing local pickup and delivery terminals are located near the intersection of two or more Interstate highways. Since hours-of-service (HOS) requirements limit a driver to eleven hours of driving per day (not including loading/unloading time), they would like each of their local terminals to be within five and a half hours travel time of a transshipment terminal (so that one driver can complete one roundtrip in a day) and, for linehaul operations between the transshipment terminals, they would like for all of the transshipment terminals to be within eleven hours of each other.

This is Model 2 with $t_{\max}$ = 11 h, on the Interstate network thinned in Sec. 4, with travel on it taken at an average of 60 mph.

The solution takes three steps: find the intersections, compute the travel time between every pair of them, and solve Model 2, after which both of its conditions are checked on the terminals it selects.

An intersection is a node of the thinned Interstate network of Code block 35 that is not the end of an Interstate, a node of degree 1. Removing an end can leave a new end behind, so the ends are removed until none is left, and the network is then thinned again:

```julia
# Code block 56: the Interstate intersections
iN, iL = tN, tL                 # the thinned network of Code block 35
while true                      # remove the ends until none is left
    deg = [count(==(k), [iL.SRC; iL.DST]) for k in 1:nrow(iN)]
    all(>(1), deg) && break     # no node of degree 1 is left
    global iN, iL = prune_reindex(iN, filter(r -> deg[r.SRC] > 1 &&
                                                deg[r.DST] > 1, iL))
end
iN, iL = prune_reindex(thin(iN, iL)...)   # remove new degree-2 nodes
nrow(iN)

```

- 1 A while loop has a scope of its own, so a variable assigned inside it is local to the loop unless it is declared otherwise. global makes this line update the iN and iL defined above the loop, so that each pass starts from the network the last pass left. Without it, in a script run as a file, such as the companion .jl, Julia would warn that the assignment is ambiguous, treat iN and iL as new variables local to the loop, and stop with an error at the loop’s first line, which reads iN before the loop has given it a value. Typed at the REPL, the loop would update them without the keyword, which does no harm there.

```text
593
```

Dividing each link’s miles by 60 mph gives its hours, and the shortest paths then give the hours between every pair of intersections, the $t_{ij}$ of Eq. 5. The implementation of Model 2 then selects the terminals for an eleven-hour day, which puts every intersection within five and a half hours of a terminal, so that one driver can drive there and back:

```julia
# Code block 57: travel times, then the terminals for an 11-hour day
gI = SimpleWeightedGraph(iL.SRC, iL.DST, iL.DIST ./ 60; combine = min)
T, _ = shortestpaths(gI, weights(gI), nv(gI))  # hours, all pairs
idx = terminals(T, 11)
length(idx)

```

- 1 The last argument is how many of the first nodes Dijkstra’s procedure is run from, and nv(gI), the number of nodes, runs it from every node, so T holds the hours between every pair of intersections.

```text
17
```

The two constraints are hard limits, so the terminals selected can be given the Bounds check of Lecture 1.2: how far any intersection lies from its nearest terminal, against five and a half hours for constraint (a), and how far any terminal lies from its nearest other terminal, against eleven for constraint (b):

```julia
# Code block 58: checking constraints (a) and (b) on the terminals
toterm = [minimum(T[i, j] for i in idx) for j in 1:nv(gI)]
near = [minimum(T[a, b] for b in idx if b != a) for a in idx]
round(maximum(toterm), digits = 2), round(maximum(near), digits = 2)
```

```text
(5.47, 10.77)
```

Every intersection is within 5.47 h of a terminal, and every terminal within 10.77 h of another.

17 transshipment terminals put every one of the 593 Interstate intersections within five and a half hours, and each terminal within eleven hours of another
